title: The forger and the detective
allegory: A GAN is like a forger and a detective training each other: the forger paints fakes from a random seed, the detective learns to tell them from the gallery's real paintings, and each one's failure is exactly the other's lesson.
map: the forger, painting from a random seed
the generator G, mapping noise z to an image
the detective's verdict: how sure it is a painting is real
the discriminator's output D(image), a probability
the forger hears only the verdict, never visits the gallery
G's gradient arrives only through D(G(z))
credit: The forger-versus-detective framing follows Goodfellow and colleagues' own analogy in the original GAN paper (2014).

chapters.name: No formula for real
chapters.note: loss = how real it looks... but how?

cap.1: You want a network that invents new pictures. But how do you score 'looks real'? There is no formula for it.
cap.2: Reconstruction-style losses tend to give blurry samples, the VAE's weakness. You want a judge of realism, and nobody can write one down by hand.
cap.3: Realism has no closed-form loss. A GAN learns the loss instead: a discriminator network is trained as the critic, and the generator is trained through it.

cap.1: So hire two rivals. A forger paints fakes from a random seed; a detective studies real paintings and fakes and says which is which. Each learns from the other.
cap.2: The generator G turns random noise z into an image. The discriminator D outputs the probability that an image is real. D trains to be right; G trains to make D wrong.
cap.3: G maps z ~ N(0, I) to an image; D maps an image to P(real). Alternating gradient steps on opposite objectives make D a learned, moving loss function for G.

cap.1: The detective's score is high when it trusts the real paintings and doubts the fakes. The detective pushes this score up; the forger pushes it down.
cap.2: D maximises V: log D(x) rewards calling real images real, log(1 − D(G(z))) rewards calling fakes fake. G only appears in the second term, and wants it low.
cap.3: min over G, max over D of E_x[log D(x)] + E_z[log(1 − D(G(z)))] (Goodfellow et al., 2014). The ideal fixed point is D = 0.5 everywhere: the detective reduced to a coin toss.

curves.label: minimise log(1 − D(G(z))): flat when losing

cap.1: Early on, the detective catches every fake. Written the original way, the forger's loss is flat there, so it learns almost nothing. Flipped, it is steep.
cap.2: When D(G(z)) is near 0, log(1 − D(G(z))) barely moves. So G maximises log D(G(z)) instead, which plunges as D(G(z)) shrinks: the strongest push when G is worst.
cap.3: Through D's sigmoid, the gradient of log(1 − D) with respect to D's logit is −D ≈ 0, while for log D it is 1 − D ≈ 1. Same equilibrium, usable gradient. The fix is in the original paper.

chapters.name: Sharp but choosy

right.title: GAN
lines: covers less: can miss whole kinds

chapters.verdict: Blurry but complete, or sharp but choosy.

cap.1: Its sibling, the VAE, paints soft, blurry pictures of everything. The GAN paints crisp pictures, but of fewer kinds of thing.
cap.2: A VAE optimises a likelihood bound and gives blurry samples; a GAN optimises against a discriminator and gives sharp but less-covered ones.
cap.3: Likelihood training penalises missing any of the data, so it spreads out; the adversarial objective penalises implausible samples, so it sharpens but can drop modes.

cap.1: The classic failure: the forger finds one painting the detective always accepts, and paints only that. Every fake is the same boat.
cap.2: Mode collapse: G maps many different z to nearly the same output because it reliably fools the current D. The symptom is a batch of near-identical samples.
cap.3: Nothing in G's objective rewards diversity; it chases D's current blind spot. The same failure returns in [2.4], where an RLHF policy collapses onto one high-reward phrasing.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: A learned judge can stand in for a loss you cannot write
Optimising against a judge finds its blind spots

cap.1: The big idea outlives GANs: when you cannot write down what 'good' means, train a judge. But anything optimised against a judge learns to exploit it.
cap.2: Reward models in RLHF are judges too, and a policy trained against one can collapse onto a single pleasing answer. Spotting the dynamic here makes it easy to spot later.
cap.3: Optimising against a learned critic recurs: reward models in RLHF, classifiers used as judges. Knowing how it fails is part of understanding and steering AI.

caption.1: Each bar is how much the best detective would trust a painting of that kind. Spread the forger evenly and every bar sits at 0.5, a coin toss. Now narrow it.
caption.2: The best detective scores each kind as real ÷ (real + fake). Collapse the forger onto boats: boats look suspicious, and the kinds it never paints look certainly real.
caption.3: For fixed G the optimal D*(x) = p_data / (p_data + p_g), from the original paper's analysis. At p_g = p_data, D* = 0.5 everywhere; under collapse D* = 1 on every mode G never paints.

where_else: RLHF: a policy optimised against a learned reward model, with the same collapse risk
Any learned judge used as a loss: classifiers, reward models, model-graded scoring
Red-teaming: searching for inputs that a judge or monitor gets wrong

hamming.what: Two networks trained against each other: a generator makes samples and a discriminator learns to tell them from real data.
hamming.when: When you cannot write a loss for 'looks real' but can collect plenty of real examples.
hamming.why: The judge becomes a learned loss that keeps getting pickier, which pushes the generator towards sharp, realistic output, and towards the judge's blind spots.

object.title: The forger's hourglass
object.subtitle: Two mirror-image networks lying end to end, touching only at the picture.

cap.1: The forger's half grows a random seed into a picture. The detective's half shrinks a picture down to one verdict.
cap.2: G upsamples noise z into an image with transposed convolutions; D downsamples an image into P(real) with strided convolutions. Mirror images.
cap.3: DCGAN conventions: kernel 4, stride 2, padding 1, so each G block doubles and each D block halves the spatial size; batchnorm everywhere except D's first and G's last block.

cap.1: They meet only at the picture. The forger never sees a real painting; it only hears the detective's verdict.
cap.2: G never touches real data. Everything it learns about realism arrives as the gradient of D's score, flowing back through D.
cap.3: G's gradient comes only via D(G(z)): real data shapes G solely by shaping D's learned decision surface.

cap.1: Detective's turn: it studies real paintings and fakes and sharpens its eye. The forger is frozen for this step.
cap.2: D step: score real x and a detached G(z), then ascend log D(x) + log(1 − D(G(z))). Detaching keeps D's update from reaching G.
cap.3: detach() cuts the graph at G(z) so D's loss produces no gradient for G; only D's optimiser steps (Adam, lr 2e-4, betas (0.5, 0.999) in DCGAN).

cap.1: Forger's turn: the verdict flows back through the detective into the forger, who adjusts. The detective itself does not change.
cap.2: G step: ascend log D(G(z)). Gradients pass through D to reach G, but only G's optimiser steps.
cap.3: In G's step, D acts as a fixed, differentiable loss; the gradient traverses it, and only G's parameters are updated.

predict.q: How many real paintings does the forger ever look at directly?

options.t: None: it learns only through the detective's verdict
All of them, on every step

predict.why: G's loss depends only on D(G(z)). Real data shapes G only by shaping D.

predict.q: The detective is winning easily: D(G(z)) is near 0. Which forger loss still gives a strong push?
predict.why: log(1 − D) is flat near D = 0 while log D plunges, so its gradient is steepest exactly when the forger is worst.

object.where: Any two-sided setup: a generator and a critic, a policy and a reward model, a red team and a monitor.
